notes:
1. Basic Facts
  • Mechanics is the branch of physics that deals with the motion, rest and equilibrium of bodies.
  • Classical mechanics mainly deals with objects moving at speeds much lower than the speed of light.
  • Mechanics is broadly divided into statics and dynamics.
  • Statics deals with bodies in equilibrium.
  • Dynamics deals with bodies in motion under the action of forces.
  • Dynamics is further divided into kinematics and kinetics.
  • Kinematics describes motion without considering its causes.
  • Kinetics studies motion together with the forces producing it.
  • Isaac Newton laid the foundation of classical mechanics.
  • Newtonian mechanics is based mainly on Newton's laws of motion and universal gravitation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mechanics → Statics + Dynamics

Dynamics → Kinematics + Kinetics

2. Statics
  • Statics is the branch of mechanics dealing with bodies in equilibrium.
  • A body in static equilibrium remains at rest.
  • For translational equilibrium, the net force on a body is zero.
  • For rotational equilibrium, the net torque on a body is zero.
  • A body can be in equilibrium even when several forces act on it if their resultant is zero.
  • Bridges, buildings and beams are analysed using principles of statics.
📌 Remember

Equilibrium → Net Force = 0 and Net Torque = 0

3. Dynamics
  • Dynamics studies bodies in motion and the causes of their motion.
  • Dynamics includes kinematics and kinetics.
  • Kinematics describes position, displacement, velocity and acceleration.
  • Kinetics relates motion to forces and mass.
  • Newton's laws form the basic framework of classical dynamics.
4. Kinematics
  • Kinematics describes motion without considering the forces causing it.
  • Important kinematic quantities include distance, displacement, speed, velocity and acceleration.
  • Motion may be translational, rotational, circular, oscillatory or random.
  • Equations of motion are used for uniformly accelerated motion.
  • Kinematics does not explain why an object accelerates.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Kinematics → How an object moves

Kinetics → Why it moves

5. Kinetics
  • Kinetics studies the relationship between motion and forces.
  • Force, mass and acceleration are central quantities in kinetics.
  • Newton's Second Law provides the basic relation F = ma for constant mass.
  • Momentum and impulse are also important in kinetics.
  • Kinetics explains changes in motion caused by forces.
6. Scalars
  • A scalar quantity has magnitude only.
  • Mass is a scalar.
  • Time is a scalar.
  • Distance is a scalar.
  • Speed is a scalar.
  • Temperature is a scalar.
  • Energy is a scalar.
  • Work is a scalar.
  • Power is a scalar.
  • Volume is a scalar.
  • Density is a scalar.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Scalar → Magnitude only

7. Vectors
  • A vector quantity has both magnitude and direction.
  • Displacement is a vector.
  • Velocity is a vector.
  • Acceleration is a vector.
  • Force is a vector.
  • Momentum is a vector.
  • Weight is a vector.
  • Torque is a vector quantity in three-dimensional mechanics.
  • Vectors are represented graphically using directed arrows.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Vector → Magnitude + Direction

8. Scalar vs Vector — Must Remember
  • Distance → Scalar.
  • Displacement → Vector.
  • Speed → Scalar.
  • Velocity → Vector.
  • Mass → Scalar.
  • Weight → Vector.
  • Energy → Scalar.
  • Momentum → Vector.
  • Work → Scalar.
  • Force → Vector.
  • Acceleration → Vector.
  • Density → Scalar.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mass ≠ Weight

Speed ≠ Velocity

Distance ≠ Displacement

9. Vector Addition
  • Vectors must be added considering both magnitude and direction.
  • Vectors in the same direction add directly.
  • Oppositely directed vectors subtract in magnitude.
  • The parallelogram law can be used to add two vectors.
  • The triangle law can also be used for vector addition.
  • The resultant vector represents the combined effect of several vectors.
10. Parallelogram Law of Vectors
  • If two vectors acting at a point are represented by adjacent sides of a parallelogram, their resultant is represented by the diagonal through that point.
  • The law is used for addition of two concurrent vectors.
  • Forces can be combined using the parallelogram law.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Parallelogram Law → Vector Addition

11. Resultant Force
  • The resultant force is a single force having the same effect as all forces acting together.
  • If forces act in the same direction, their magnitudes are added.
  • If forces act in opposite directions, their magnitudes are subtracted.
  • Zero resultant force implies no acceleration.
  • A zero resultant force does not necessarily mean that no forces act.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Net force = 0 does not mean force = absent.

It means forces are balanced.

12. Resolution of Forces
  • A force can be resolved into components.
  • Rectangular components are usually taken along mutually perpendicular axes.
  • For a force F making angle θ with the horizontal:
  • Horizontal component = F cos θ.
  • Vertical component = F sin θ.
  • Resolution simplifies analysis of forces acting at angles.
13. Equilibrium
  • A body is in equilibrium when there is no net change in its translational or rotational motion.
  • Translational equilibrium requires net force to be zero.
  • Rotational equilibrium requires net torque to be zero.
  • Static equilibrium refers to a body at rest.
  • Dynamic equilibrium may refer to a body moving with constant velocity when net force is zero.
📌 Remember

ΣF = 0

Στ = 0

14. Types of Equilibrium
  • Stable equilibrium occurs when a displaced body tends to return to its original position.
  • Unstable equilibrium occurs when a displaced body moves farther from its original position.
  • Neutral equilibrium occurs when a displaced body remains in its new position.
  • A ball at the bottom of a bowl shows stable equilibrium.
  • A ball balanced on top of a hill shows unstable equilibrium.
  • A ball on a horizontal surface approximates neutral equilibrium.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Stable → Returns

Unstable → Moves away

Neutral → Stays in new position

15. Centre of Gravity
  • The centre of gravity is the point through which the resultant gravitational force on a body may be considered to act.
  • In a uniform gravitational field, centre of gravity approximately coincides with centre of mass.
  • A body is more stable when its centre of gravity is lower.
  • A wider base generally increases stability.
  • A body topples when the vertical line through its centre of gravity falls outside its base of support.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Greater Stability → Low Centre of Gravity + Wide Base

16. Centre of Mass
  • Centre of mass is the point representing the average position of mass in a system.
  • Motion of the centre of mass depends on the net external force.
  • Internal forces cannot change the motion of the centre of mass of an isolated system.
  • For a uniform symmetrical body, the centre of mass is usually at its geometrical centre.
  • Centre of mass need not always lie within the physical material of an object.
Example

For a uniform ring, the centre of mass lies at its centre, where there is no material.

17. Mass
  • Mass is the quantity of matter and a measure of inertia.
  • The SI unit of mass is kilogram.
  • Mass is a scalar quantity.
  • Mass remains essentially constant irrespective of location in ordinary mechanics.
  • Greater mass means greater resistance to acceleration for a given force.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Mass → Inertia → kilogram

18. Weight
  • Weight is the gravitational force acting on a body.
  • Weight is given by W = mg.
  • m is mass.
  • g is acceleration due to gravity.
  • The SI unit of weight is newton.
  • Weight is a vector quantity.
  • Weight varies when gravitational acceleration changes.
  • An object's mass on the Moon remains nearly the same as on Earth, but its weight changes.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mass → kg

Weight → N

19. Weight on the Moon
  • Gravitational acceleration on the Moon is about one-sixth of that on Earth.
  • Therefore, an object's weight on the Moon is approximately one-sixth its weight on Earth.
  • Its mass remains unchanged.
📌 Remember

Moon weight ≈ Earth weight / 6

20. Inertia
  • Inertia is the tendency of a body to resist a change in its state of motion.
  • Mass is a measure of inertia.
  • A body at rest tends to remain at rest.
  • A moving body tends to continue with constant velocity unless acted on by a net external force.
  • Newton's First Law is called the Law of Inertia.
21. Force
  • Force is a push or pull capable of changing motion or shape.
  • Force is a vector quantity.
  • SI unit of force is newton.
  • One newton equals 1 kg m/s².
  • Forces may be contact or non-contact forces.
  • A net force produces acceleration.
22. Contact Forces
  • Contact forces require physical contact between bodies.
  • Friction is a contact force.
  • Normal reaction is a contact force.
  • Tension is a contact force.
  • Spring force is a contact force.
  • Air resistance is a contact force because it results from interactions with air molecules.
23. Non-Contact Forces
  • Non-contact forces act without direct physical contact.
  • Gravitational force is a non-contact force.
  • Electrostatic force is a non-contact force.
  • Magnetic force can act without direct contact.
  • These forces act through physical fields.
24. Normal Reaction
  • Normal reaction is the force exerted by a surface perpendicular to itself.
  • The normal force does not always equal the weight.
  • On a horizontal surface with no other vertical forces, normal reaction may equal weight.
  • On an inclined plane, the normal component differs from the full weight.
  • Normal force contributes to friction in many models.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Normal reaction ≠ always mg

25. Tension
  • Tension is a pulling force transmitted through a string, rope or cable.
  • Ideal light strings are often assumed to have uniform tension.
  • Tension acts along the length of a string.
  • A string can pull but cannot normally push.
26. Friction
  • Friction opposes relative motion or tendency of relative motion between surfaces.
  • Static friction acts before sliding begins.
  • Limiting friction is the maximum static friction.
  • Sliding or kinetic friction acts when surfaces slide.
  • Rolling friction is generally less than sliding friction.
  • Friction can be useful or undesirable.
  • Walking depends on friction.
  • Vehicle brakes depend on friction.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Rolling Friction < Sliding Friction in general

27. Coefficient of Friction
  • Coefficient of friction is a dimensionless quantity.
  • It is commonly represented by μ.
  • Limiting friction is approximately μN in the simple dry-friction model.
  • N is normal reaction.
  • The coefficient depends on the nature and condition of surfaces.
  • It has no SI unit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Coefficient of friction → No unit

28. Reducing Friction
  • Lubrication reduces friction between moving surfaces.
  • Ball bearings reduce sliding friction by replacing it largely with rolling friction.
  • Polishing surfaces can reduce surface irregularities in suitable situations.
  • Streamlining reduces fluid resistance.
  • Air cushions can reduce direct surface contact.
29. Increasing Friction
  • Tyre treads increase grip.
  • Rough surfaces increase friction in many situations.
  • Spikes in athletic shoes improve grip.
  • Sand may be spread on slippery surfaces to increase friction.
  • Brake pads are designed to provide friction.
30. Fluid Friction
  • Fluids resist the motion of objects through them.
  • Fluid resistance is also called drag.
  • Air resistance is a form of drag.
  • Drag generally increases with speed.
  • Streamlining helps reduce drag.
  • Viscosity contributes to internal fluid resistance.
31. Viscosity
  • Viscosity is the internal resistance of a fluid to flow.
  • A highly viscous fluid flows less easily.
  • Honey is more viscous than water at ordinary conditions.
  • The SI unit of dynamic viscosity is pascal-second.
  • Viscosity of liquids generally decreases as temperature increases.
  • Viscosity of gases generally increases with temperature.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Liquids: Temperature ↑ → Viscosity generally ↓

Gases: Temperature ↑ → Viscosity generally ↑

32. Terminal Velocity
  • Terminal velocity is the constant maximum speed reached by a falling body moving through a fluid.
  • At terminal velocity, net force becomes zero.
  • Weight is balanced by drag and buoyancy.
  • Acceleration becomes zero at terminal velocity.
  • Parachutes reduce terminal velocity by increasing air resistance.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Terminal Velocity → Net Force = 0 → Acceleration = 0

33. Pressure
  • Pressure is force acting per unit area.
  • Pressure = Force/Area.
  • P = F/A.
  • The SI unit of pressure is pascal.
  • One pascal equals one newton per square metre.
  • Pressure is a scalar quantity.
  • For the same force, smaller area produces greater pressure.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Pressure → P = F/A → pascal

34. Applications of Pressure
  • A sharp knife cuts efficiently because force acts over a small area.
  • Needles have pointed ends to produce high pressure.
  • Broad straps reduce pressure on the shoulder by increasing area.
  • Tractors use wide tyres to reduce pressure on soft soil.
  • Snowshoes reduce pressure by increasing contact area.
35. Pressure in Liquids
  • Pressure in a liquid increases with depth.
  • Liquid pressure depends on density.
  • Hydrostatic pressure is given by P = ρgh for a liquid column.
  • ρ is density.
  • g is gravitational acceleration.
  • h is depth.
  • At the same depth in the same connected liquid at rest, pressure is equal.
  • Liquid pressure acts in all directions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Liquid Pressure → ρgh

36. Pascal's Principle
  • Pressure applied to an enclosed fluid is transmitted equally throughout the fluid.
  • Hydraulic machines use Pascal's principle.
  • Hydraulic brakes are an application.
  • Hydraulic lifts are an application.
  • Hydraulic presses are an application.
37. Hydraulic Machines
  • Hydraulic machines multiply force using differences in piston area.
  • Pressure on the small piston is transmitted to the large piston.
  • F₁/A₁ = F₂/A₂ in an ideal hydraulic system.
  • A large output force can be obtained using a smaller input force.
  • Mechanical advantage is obtained at the expense of greater movement distance of the smaller piston.
38. Buoyancy
  • Buoyancy is the upward force exerted by a fluid on an immersed body.
  • Buoyant force arises from differences in fluid pressure with depth.
  • Archimedes' Principle gives the magnitude of buoyant force.
  • Buoyant force equals the weight of displaced fluid.
  • Buoyancy acts in liquids and gases.
39. Archimedes' Principle
  • A body wholly or partially immersed in a fluid experiences an upward force.
  • The upward force equals the weight of fluid displaced.
  • Archimedes' Principle explains floating and apparent loss of weight in fluids.
  • It is used in hydrometers and ship design.
40. Apparent Weight
  • Apparent weight of an immersed object is less than its actual weight because of buoyant force.
  • Apparent weight = Actual weight − Buoyant force.
  • A fully submerged body may still sink if its weight exceeds the buoyant force.
41. Relative Density
  • Relative density is the ratio of the density of a substance to the density of a reference substance.
  • For solids and liquids, water is commonly used as the reference.
  • Relative density has no unit.
  • A substance with relative density less than 1 tends to float on water if other conditions permit.
  • A hydrometer measures relative density of liquids.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Relative Density → No unit

Hydrometer → Relative density of liquids

42. Density
  • Density is mass per unit volume.
  • ρ = m/V.
  • The SI unit of density is kg/m³.
  • Density is a scalar quantity.
  • An object floats when its average density is sufficiently lower than that of the surrounding fluid.
  • Density generally changes with temperature because volume changes.
43. Floating Bodies
  • A floating body displaces a weight of fluid equal to its own weight.
  • For floating equilibrium, buoyant force equals weight.
  • A body with average density less than the fluid generally floats.
  • A body denser than the fluid generally sinks unless other effects provide support.
  • Ships float because their hollow shape lowers their overall average density.
44. Submarine
  • A submarine controls its buoyancy using ballast tanks.
  • Taking water into ballast tanks increases average density.
  • Expelling water and replacing it with air decreases average density.
  • Neutral buoyancy allows a submarine to remain at approximately constant depth.
45. Hydrometer
  • A hydrometer measures the relative density or specific gravity of liquids.
  • It works on the principle of floatation.
  • A hydrometer sinks deeper in a less dense liquid.
  • It floats higher in a denser liquid.
  • Lactometers are specialised hydrometers used to estimate milk density.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Hydrometer → Relative Density

Lactometer → Milk

46. Moment of Force
  • Moment of force is the turning effect of a force.
  • Moment = Force × perpendicular distance from pivot.
  • Moment is also called torque in elementary mechanics.
  • SI unit is newton metre.
  • A longer spanner produces greater torque for the same force.
  • Door handles are placed far from hinges to increase turning effect.
47. Torque
  • Torque is the rotational effect of a force.
  • τ = r × F in vector form.
  • Magnitude is τ = rF sin θ.
  • Torque depends on force and perpendicular lever arm.
  • Net torque produces angular acceleration.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Torque → Turning Effect

48. Couple
  • A couple consists of two equal and opposite parallel forces separated by a distance.
  • The net force of a couple is zero.
  • A couple produces pure rotation.
  • Moment of a couple = One force × perpendicular distance between the forces.
  • Turning a steering wheel with two hands can approximate the action of a couple.
49. Principle of Moments
  • For rotational equilibrium, sum of clockwise moments equals sum of anticlockwise moments.
  • The principle is used in balances and levers.
  • It follows from the condition of zero net torque.
📌 Remember

Clockwise Moment = Anticlockwise Moment

50. Lever
  • A lever is a rigid bar that can rotate about a fixed point.
  • The fixed point is called the fulcrum.
  • Effort is the applied force.
  • Load is the resistance being moved.
  • Effort arm is the distance from fulcrum to effort.
  • Load arm is the distance from fulcrum to load.
  • Levers can provide mechanical advantage.
51. Law of Lever
  • For an ideal lever in equilibrium:
  • Effort × Effort arm = Load × Load arm.
  • Mechanical advantage = Load/Effort.
  • Longer effort arm can reduce the effort required.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Lever → Effort × Effort Arm = Load × Load Arm

52. First-Class Lever
  • In a first-class lever, fulcrum lies between effort and load.
  • A seesaw is a first-class lever.
  • Scissors act as first-class levers.
  • Pliers are first-class levers.
  • A crowbar can act as a first-class lever.
  • Mechanical advantage may be greater than, equal to or less than 1 depending on arm lengths.
📌 Memory

First Class → Fulcrum in middle

53. Second-Class Lever
  • In a second-class lever, load lies between fulcrum and effort.
  • A wheelbarrow is a second-class lever.
  • A nutcracker is a second-class lever.
  • A bottle opener can act as a second-class lever.
  • Mechanical advantage is generally greater than 1.
📌 Memory

Second Class → Load in middle

54. Third-Class Lever
  • In a third-class lever, effort lies between fulcrum and load.
  • Human forearm with biceps is a common third-class lever.
  • Tweezers can act as third-class levers.
  • A fishing rod can function as a third-class lever.
  • Mechanical advantage is generally less than 1.
  • Third-class levers favour speed and range of motion rather than force multiplication.
📌 Memory

Third Class → Effort in middle

55. Lever Mnemonic
  • First class → Fulcrum in middle.
  • Second class → Load in middle.
  • Third class → Effort in middle.
📌 Remember

FLE

First → Fulcrum

Second → Load

Third → Effort

56. Mechanical Advantage
  • Mechanical advantage is the ratio of load to effort.
  • MA = Load/Effort.
  • Mechanical advantage greater than 1 means force multiplication.
  • Mechanical advantage has no unit.
  • Ideal machines can trade force for distance.
57. Velocity Ratio
  • Velocity ratio is the distance moved by effort divided by distance moved by load.
  • VR = Distance moved by effort / Distance moved by load.
  • Velocity ratio depends mainly on machine geometry.
  • Velocity ratio has no unit.
58. Efficiency
  • Efficiency is the ratio of useful output work to input work.
  • Efficiency = Output/Input × 100%.
  • Efficiency is dimensionless.
  • No real machine is 100% efficient because some energy is dissipated.
  • Friction is a common cause of reduced efficiency.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Efficiency = MA/VR × 100% for simple machines

59. Simple Machines
  • Simple machines make work easier by changing the magnitude or direction of force.
  • The six classical simple machines are lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw.
  • Simple machines do not create energy.
  • Ideal machines conserve work.
  • Real machines lose some useful energy mainly through friction.
📌 Must-Memorise

Lever

Wheel and axle

Pulley

Inclined plane

Wedge

Screw

60. Inclined Plane
  • An inclined plane is a sloping surface used to raise or lower loads.
  • It reduces the force required by increasing the distance over which the force acts.
  • Ramps are inclined planes.
  • An ideal inclined plane does not reduce total work; it trades force for distance.
61. Wedge
  • A wedge consists essentially of two inclined planes joined together.
  • Wedges convert applied force into forces directed sideways.
  • Knives and axes function as wedges.
  • Needles are wedge-like tools.
  • A sharper wedge concentrates force over a smaller area.
62. Screw
  • A screw is an inclined plane wrapped around a cylinder.
  • The helical ridge is called the thread.
  • Screws convert rotational motion into linear motion.
  • A screw jack provides large mechanical advantage.
  • Smaller thread pitch generally increases mechanical advantage but requires more turns.
63. Wheel and Axle
  • A wheel and axle consists of a large wheel fixed to a smaller axle.
  • Turning the wheel can produce greater force at the axle.
  • Door knobs operate using the wheel-and-axle principle.
  • Steering wheels provide torque using a large radius.
  • The mechanical advantage depends on the ratio of radii.
64. Pulley
  • A pulley consists of a grooved wheel with a rope or cable.
  • A fixed pulley mainly changes the direction of force.
  • An ideal single fixed pulley has mechanical advantage 1.
  • A movable pulley can provide force multiplication.
  • Systems of pulleys are called block and tackle arrangements.
  • Mechanical advantage increases with the number of supporting rope segments in an ideal arrangement.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Fixed Pulley → Changes direction

Movable Pulley → Force advantage

65. Work
  • Work is done when a force causes displacement.
  • Work = Force × displacement in the direction of force.
  • W = Fs cos θ.
  • SI unit of work is joule.
  • One joule equals one newton metre.
  • Work is a scalar quantity.
  • No mechanical work is done if there is no displacement.
  • Work can be positive, negative or zero.
66. Positive, Negative and Zero Work
  • Positive work occurs when force has a component in the direction of displacement.
  • Negative work occurs when force opposes displacement.
  • Friction usually does negative work on a moving body.
  • Zero work occurs when force is perpendicular to displacement.
  • In ideal uniform circular motion, centripetal force does zero work because it is perpendicular to instantaneous displacement.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Force may act even when mechanical work is zero.

67. Power
  • Power is the rate of doing work.
  • Power = Work/Time.
  • P = W/t.
  • SI unit is watt.
  • One watt equals one joule per second.
  • Power is a scalar quantity.
  • Greater power means the same work can be done in less time.
68. Horsepower
  • Horsepower is a non-SI unit of power.
  • One mechanical horsepower is approximately 746 watts.
  • James Watt popularised the use of horsepower as a measure of engine power.
  • The SI unit of power remains watt.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

1 hp ≈ 746 W

69. Energy
  • Energy is the capacity to do work.
  • SI unit of energy is joule.
  • Mechanical energy includes kinetic and potential energy.
  • Energy is a scalar quantity.
  • Energy can be transformed from one form to another.
  • Total energy is conserved in an isolated system.
70. Kinetic Energy
  • Kinetic energy is energy due to motion.
  • KE = ½mv².
  • Kinetic energy depends on mass.
  • Kinetic energy depends on the square of velocity.
  • Doubling velocity makes kinetic energy four times larger for the same mass.
📌 Remember

v × 2 → KE × 4

71. Potential Energy
  • Potential energy is energy due to position or configuration.
  • Near Earth's surface, gravitational potential energy is mgh.
  • Elastic potential energy is stored in stretched or compressed springs.
  • Potential energy can convert into kinetic energy.
72. Mechanical Energy
  • Mechanical energy is the sum of kinetic and potential energies.
  • In an ideal system without dissipative forces, mechanical energy remains constant.
  • Friction converts some mechanical energy into thermal energy.
  • Conservation of total energy still applies even when mechanical energy decreases.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Mechanical energy may decrease due to friction.

Total energy is still conserved.

73. Momentum
  • Momentum is mass multiplied by velocity.
  • p = mv.
  • Momentum is a vector quantity.
  • SI unit is kg m/s.
  • Momentum increases with both mass and velocity.
  • Total momentum remains constant in an isolated system.
74. Impulse
  • Impulse is the product of force and the time for which it acts.
  • Impulse = FΔt for constant force.
  • Impulse equals change in momentum.
  • J = Δp.
  • SI unit of impulse is N s.
  • N s is equivalent to kg m/s.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Impulse → Change in Momentum

75. Applications of Impulse
  • Airbags increase collision time and reduce average force.
  • Seat belts increase stopping time and reduce injury risk.
  • A cricketer moves the hands backward while catching to increase stopping time.
  • Sand pits reduce force on landing by increasing stopping distance and time.
  • Helmets absorb energy and extend collision time.
76. Collision
  • A collision is an interaction in which bodies exert large forces on each other over a short time.
  • Momentum is conserved in an isolated collision.
  • Elastic collisions conserve both momentum and kinetic energy.
  • Inelastic collisions conserve momentum but not kinetic energy.
  • In a perfectly inelastic collision, bodies stick together.
77. Elastic Collision
  • Total momentum is conserved.
  • Total kinetic energy is conserved.
  • Ideal elastic collisions occur approximately between some microscopic particles.
  • Macroscopic collisions are rarely perfectly elastic.
78. Inelastic Collision
  • Momentum is conserved in an isolated inelastic collision.
  • Kinetic energy is not conserved as kinetic energy.
  • Some kinetic energy becomes heat, sound or deformation.
  • In a perfectly inelastic collision, objects move together afterward.
79. Circular Motion
  • Circular motion is motion along a circular path.
  • Even at constant speed, velocity changes because direction changes.
  • Therefore, circular motion involves acceleration.
  • Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the centre.
  • Centripetal force is the net inward force producing circular motion.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Constant speed in a circle ≠ Zero acceleration

80. Centripetal Acceleration
  • Centripetal acceleration is directed toward the centre of a circular path.
  • a = v²/r.
  • Greater speed produces greater centripetal acceleration.
  • Larger radius reduces centripetal acceleration for the same speed.
81. Centripetal Force
  • Centripetal force is the resultant inward force required for circular motion.
  • F = mv²/r.
  • Centripetal force is not a new type of fundamental force.
  • Gravity can provide centripetal force for planetary motion.
  • Friction can provide centripetal force for a vehicle turning on a road.
  • Tension can provide centripetal force for an object moving in a circle on a string.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

“Centripetal force” describes the role of the inward resultant force, not a separate fundamental interaction.

82. Centrifugal Effect
  • In a rotating reference frame, an apparent outward centrifugal force may be introduced.
  • Centrifugal force is a pseudo or inertial force in the rotating frame.
  • In an inertial frame, circular motion is explained using inward centripetal force.
  • Passengers feel pushed outward during a turn because of inertia and the rotating frame.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Centripetal → Real inward resultant in inertial frame

Centrifugal → Apparent outward force in rotating frame

83. Banking of Roads
  • Roads are banked at curves to help vehicles turn safely.
  • Banking allows a component of normal reaction to contribute to centripetal force.
  • Banking reduces dependence on friction.
  • Proper banking is especially important for high-speed curves.
84. Rotational Motion
  • Rotational motion is motion about an axis.
  • Angular displacement describes rotational position.
  • Angular velocity is rate of change of angular displacement.
  • Angular acceleration is rate of change of angular velocity.
  • Torque produces angular acceleration.
  • Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass.
85. Angular Velocity
  • Angular velocity is the rate of change of angular displacement.
  • It is represented by ω.
  • SI unit is radian per second.
  • For uniform circular motion, v = rω.
  • All points on a rigid rotating body have the same angular velocity but different linear speeds depending on radius.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

v = rω

86. Moment of Inertia
  • Moment of inertia measures resistance to change in rotational motion.
  • It depends on total mass.
  • It also depends on how mass is distributed relative to the axis.
  • Mass farther from the axis increases moment of inertia.
  • Moment of inertia is the rotational analogue of mass.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Linear → Mass

Rotational → Moment of Inertia

87. Angular Momentum
  • Angular momentum is the rotational analogue of linear momentum.
  • For a rigid body rotating about a fixed axis, L = Iω.
  • I is moment of inertia.
  • ω is angular velocity.
  • Angular momentum is conserved when external torque is zero.
88. Conservation of Angular Momentum
  • Angular momentum remains constant when no external torque acts.
  • A skater spins faster by pulling the arms inward.
  • Pulling arms inward decreases moment of inertia.
  • Angular velocity increases to conserve angular momentum.
  • Planetary motion also obeys angular-momentum conservation.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

I ↓ → ω ↑ when L is constant

89. Simple Harmonic Motion
  • Simple harmonic motion is periodic motion in which restoring force is proportional to displacement and directed toward equilibrium.
  • A mass-spring system can perform simple harmonic motion.
  • A simple pendulum approximates simple harmonic motion for small angles.
  • Displacement, velocity and acceleration vary periodically.
  • Acceleration is maximum at extreme positions.
  • Velocity is maximum at the equilibrium position.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

SHM at equilibrium → Velocity maximum, acceleration zero.

At extreme position → Velocity zero, acceleration maximum.

90. Simple Pendulum
  • A simple pendulum consists ideally of a point mass suspended by a light inextensible string.
  • For small oscillations, T = 2π√(L/g).
  • Time period depends on pendulum length.
  • Time period depends on gravitational acceleration.
  • Time period does not depend on bob mass for an ideal simple pendulum.
  • Longer pendulum → Longer period.
  • Greater g → Shorter period.
91. Frequency
  • Frequency is the number of complete oscillations per unit time.
  • SI unit of frequency is hertz.
  • One hertz equals one cycle per second.
  • Frequency f = 1/T.
  • T is time period.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

f = 1/T

92. Time Period
  • Time period is the time taken for one complete cycle.
  • SI unit is second.
  • Time period and frequency are reciprocals.
  • T = 1/f.
93. Resonance
  • Resonance occurs when an external periodic force has frequency near a system's natural frequency.
  • Resonance can produce large-amplitude oscillations.
  • Musical instruments use resonance.
  • Bridges and buildings must be designed to avoid dangerous resonance.
  • Soldiers may be instructed to break step while crossing certain bridges to reduce risk of synchronized forcing.
94. Elasticity
  • Elasticity is the property of a material to regain its original shape after removal of deforming force.
  • Perfect elasticity is an idealisation.
  • Elastic deformation is reversible.
  • Plastic deformation is permanent.
  • Hooke's Law applies within the proportional or elastic range depending on context.
95. Stress
  • Stress is restoring force per unit area.
  • Stress has the same SI unit as pressure.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • Stress can be tensile, compressive or shear.
  • Stress is generated when a material is deformed.
96. Strain
  • Strain is the fractional change in dimension.
  • Longitudinal strain = Change in length / Original length.
  • Strain is dimensionless.
  • Strain has no SI unit.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Stress → Unit Pa

Strain → No unit

97. Young's Modulus
  • Young's modulus is the ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain within the elastic range.
  • A larger Young's modulus generally indicates a stiffer material.
  • SI unit is pascal.
  • It is an elastic modulus.
98. Elastic Limit
  • Elastic limit is the maximum stress up to which a material returns to its original form after the force is removed.
  • Beyond the elastic limit, permanent deformation may occur.
  • Hooke's proportionality is valid only over a limited range.
99. Projectile Motion
  • Projectile motion is motion under gravity after an object is launched, neglecting air resistance.
  • Horizontal motion has constant velocity in the ideal model.
  • Vertical motion has constant downward acceleration g.
  • The ideal trajectory is a parabola.
  • Horizontal and vertical motions are analysed independently.
  • At the highest point, vertical velocity is zero.
  • Horizontal velocity remains non-zero in ideal projectile motion.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

At highest point of projectile:

Vertical velocity = 0

Acceleration ≠ 0

Acceleration = g downward

100. Range of Projectile
  • For launch and landing at the same level without air resistance, range R = u² sin 2θ/g.
  • Maximum range occurs at 45° for a given launch speed on level ground.
  • Complementary launch angles θ and 90° − θ give the same range under ideal conditions.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Maximum range → 45°

101. Free Fall
  • Free fall is motion under the influence of gravity alone.
  • In vacuum, all bodies fall with the same acceleration regardless of mass.
  • Near Earth's surface, g is approximately 9.8 m/s².
  • Galileo's work helped establish the principle that falling acceleration is independent of mass in the absence of air resistance.
  • Air resistance causes different objects to fall differently in normal atmospheric conditions.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Heavier bodies do not fall faster in vacuum simply because they are heavier.

102. Acceleration Due to Gravity
  • Acceleration due to gravity is represented by g.
  • Near Earth's surface, g is approximately 9.8 m/s².
  • g varies slightly with latitude, altitude and depth.
  • g is greater near the poles than near the equator.
  • g decreases with increasing altitude.
  • g decreases as one moves toward Earth's centre.
  • At Earth's centre, net gravitational acceleration is approximately zero.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

g at Earth's centre → 0

103. Escape Velocity
  • Escape velocity is the minimum speed required to escape from a body's gravitational field without further propulsion.
  • Earth's escape velocity is about 11.2 km/s.
  • Escape velocity is independent of the mass of the escaping object in the ideal model.
  • Escape velocity increases with the mass of the planet.
  • Escape velocity decreases with increasing distance from the planet's centre.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Earth Escape Velocity → 11.2 km/s

104. Orbital Velocity
  • Orbital velocity is the speed required for an object to maintain a stable orbit at a given radius.
  • Near Earth's surface in an ideal low orbit, orbital speed is roughly 7.9 km/s.
  • Orbital velocity is lower than Earth's surface escape velocity.
  • Satellites remain in orbit by continuously falling around Earth.
📌 Remember

Near-Earth orbital speed → ~7.9 km/s

Escape speed → ~11.2 km/s

105. Geostationary Orbit
  • A geostationary satellite appears stationary relative to an observer on Earth.
  • It orbits above the equator.
  • It moves in the same direction as Earth's rotation.
  • Its orbital period is approximately 24 hours.
  • Its altitude is approximately 35,786 km above the equator.
  • Geostationary satellites are useful for communication and weather observation.
106. Mechanical Advantage of Machines
  • Machines cannot multiply energy.
  • Machines can multiply force by increasing the distance through which effort moves.
  • Mechanical advantage greater than 1 means output force exceeds input force.
  • A machine with mechanical advantage less than 1 may provide speed or distance advantage.
  • Ideal input work equals ideal output work.
⚠️ TNPSC Trap

Machine → Can multiply force.

Machine → Cannot create energy.

107. Ideal Machine
  • An ideal machine has no energy loss.
  • Efficiency of an ideal machine is 100%.
  • In an ideal machine, input work equals output work.
  • Real machines are less than 100% efficient.
  • Friction is a major source of energy loss in machines.
108. Newton — Important Mechanics Facts
  • Isaac Newton was born in 1642 according to the old-style English calendar, corresponding to 1643 in the modern Gregorian calendar.
  • Newton published Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica in 1687.
  • The work is commonly called the Principia.
  • Newton formulated three laws of motion.
  • Newton formulated the universal law of gravitation.
  • Newton's work provided a mathematical foundation for classical mechanics.
  • The SI unit of force, newton, is named after him.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Newton → Principia → 1687 → Classical Mechanics

109. Galileo — Mechanics Facts
  • Galileo Galilei made major contributions to the study of motion.
  • He investigated falling bodies.
  • He studied acceleration.
  • Galileo challenged the belief that heavier bodies necessarily fall faster.
  • His work laid foundations for classical kinematics.
  • Galileo also studied projectile motion.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Galileo → Falling Bodies + Projectile Motion

110. Archimedes — Mechanics Facts
  • Archimedes was an ancient Greek mathematician and scientist.
  • He formulated the principle of buoyancy bearing his name.
  • Archimedes also studied levers.
  • The statement “Give me a place to stand and I will move the Earth” is traditionally associated with his work on levers.
  • Archimedes made important contributions to hydrostatics.
🔗 TNPSC Key Link

Archimedes → Lever + Buoyancy

111. Important Mechanics Formulae
  • Pressure → P = F/A.
  • Density → ρ = m/V.
  • Weight → W = mg.
  • Force → F = ma.
  • Momentum → p = mv.
  • Impulse → J = Δp.
  • Work → W = Fs cos θ.
  • Power → P = W/t.
  • Kinetic energy → KE = ½mv².
  • Gravitational potential energy → PE = mgh.
  • Centripetal acceleration → a = v²/r.
  • Centripetal force → F = mv²/r.
  • Moment → Force × perpendicular distance.
  • Angular momentum → L = Iω.
  • Linear-angular velocity → v = rω.
  • Frequency → f = 1/T.
  • Simple pendulum → T = 2π√(L/g).
  • Liquid pressure → P = ρgh.
  • Projectile range → R = u² sin 2θ/g.
112. Important SI Units
  • Length → metre.
  • Mass → kilogram.
  • Time → second.
  • Force → newton.
  • Work → joule.
  • Energy → joule.
  • Power → watt.
  • Pressure → pascal.
  • Momentum → kg m/s.
  • Impulse → N s.
  • Torque → N m.
  • Density → kg/m³.
  • Frequency → hertz.
  • Angular velocity → rad/s.
  • Stress → pascal.
  • Strain → No unit.
  • Mechanical advantage → No unit.
  • Efficiency → No unit or expressed as percentage.
  • Coefficient of friction → No unit.
  • Relative density → No unit.
113. Important Derived Units
  • 1 newton = 1 kg m/s².
  • 1 joule = 1 N m.
  • 1 watt = 1 J/s.
  • 1 pascal = 1 N/m².
  • 1 hertz = 1 s⁻¹.
  • 1 N s = 1 kg m/s.
114. Must-Memorise Mechanics Pairs
  • Statics → Equilibrium.
  • Kinematics → Description of motion.
  • Kinetics → Forces causing motion.
  • Scalar → Magnitude only.
  • Vector → Magnitude + direction.
  • Mass → Inertia.
  • Weight → Gravitational force.
  • Friction → Opposes relative motion.
  • Torque → Turning effect.
  • Impulse → Change in momentum.
  • Power → Rate of doing work.
  • Density → Mass/Volume.
  • Pressure → Force/Area.
  • Buoyancy → Upward fluid force.
  • Hydrometer → Relative density.
  • Lactometer → Milk density.
  • Centripetal force → Inward.
  • Resonance → Driving frequency near natural frequency.
115. TNPSC Traps
  • Mechanics is broader than motion alone.
  • Statics deals with equilibrium; dynamics deals with motion.
  • Kinematics does not study forces causing motion.
  • Distance is scalar; displacement is vector.
  • Speed is scalar; velocity is vector.
  • Mass is scalar; weight is vector.
  • Mass remains constant while weight varies with g.
  • Weight on Moon is about one-sixth Earth weight.
  • Net force zero does not mean no forces are acting.
  • A moving body can have zero net force if velocity is constant.
  • Normal force is not always equal to weight.
  • Friction is not always harmful.
  • Rolling friction is generally less than sliding friction.
  • Coefficient of friction has no unit.
  • Pressure increases when the same force acts over a smaller area.
  • Liquid pressure increases with depth.
  • Relative density has no unit.
  • A hydrometer measures liquid density or relative density.
  • A lactometer is used for milk.
  • Torque unit is N m, but torque is not normally expressed as joule.
  • Mechanical advantage has no unit.
  • A fixed pulley mainly changes direction of force.
  • A movable pulley can provide mechanical advantage.
  • Machines do not create energy.
  • Work is zero if there is no displacement.
  • Centripetal force does no work in ideal uniform circular motion.
  • Momentum is vector; kinetic energy is scalar.
  • Momentum is conserved in isolated elastic and inelastic collisions.
  • Kinetic energy is conserved only in elastic collisions.
  • Constant circular speed still involves acceleration.
  • Centripetal acceleration is toward the centre.
  • Centrifugal force is a pseudo force in a rotating frame.
  • At the highest point of projectile motion, vertical velocity is zero but acceleration is not zero.
  • In vacuum, all bodies fall with the same gravitational acceleration.
  • At Earth's centre, g is approximately zero.
  • Escape velocity on Earth is about 11.2 km/s.
  • Orbital velocity near Earth is about 7.9 km/s.
  • Stress has a unit; strain does not.
  • Simple-pendulum period does not depend on bob mass in the ideal small-angle approximation.
116. Ultra-Short Memory Chain
  • Mechanics → Motion + Equilibrium.
  • Statics → Rest/equilibrium.
  • Dynamics → Motion.
  • Kinematics → Motion description.
  • Kinetics → Motion + force.
  • Scalar → Magnitude.
  • Vector → Magnitude + direction.
  • Mass → kg.
  • Weight → mg.
  • Force → N.
  • Pressure → F/A.
  • Density → m/V.
  • Friction → Opposes motion.
  • Buoyancy → Upward force.
  • Archimedes → Displaced fluid.
  • Pascal → Hydraulic machines.
  • Torque → Turning effect.
  • Lever → Fulcrum.
  • MA → Load/Effort.
  • Work → Force × displacement.
  • Power → Work/time.
  • KE → ½mv².
  • PE → mgh.
  • Momentum → mv.
  • Impulse → Δp.
  • Circular motion → Centripetal force.
  • Rotation → Torque.
  • SHM → Restoring force.
  • Pendulum → 2π√(L/g).
  • Stress → Force/area.
  • Strain → Fractional deformation.
  • Projectile → Parabolic path.
  • Earth g → 9.8 m/s².
  • Orbital speed → ~7.9 km/s.
  • Escape speed → ~11.2 km/s.
Rapid Revision — TNPSC Most Expected
  • Branch of physics dealing with motion and equilibrium? → Mechanics.
  • Two broad divisions of mechanics? → Statics and dynamics.
  • Branch dealing with equilibrium? → Statics.
  • Branch dealing with motion? → Dynamics.
  • Dynamics is divided into? → Kinematics and kinetics.
  • Kinematics studies? → Motion without considering its causes.
  • Kinetics studies? → Motion and forces causing it.
  • Quantity having magnitude only? → Scalar.
  • Quantity having magnitude and direction? → Vector.
  • Distance is? → Scalar.
  • Displacement is? → Vector.
  • Speed is? → Scalar.
  • Velocity is? → Vector.
  • Mass is? → Scalar.
  • Weight is? → Vector.
  • Force is? → Vector.
  • Work is? → Scalar.
  • Momentum is? → Vector.
  • Condition for translational equilibrium? → Net force = 0.
  • Condition for rotational equilibrium? → Net torque = 0.
  • Equilibrium in which body returns after displacement? → Stable equilibrium.
  • Equilibrium in which body moves farther away? → Unstable equilibrium.
  • Equilibrium in which body remains in new position? → Neutral equilibrium.
  • Greater stability is obtained by? → Lower centre of gravity and wider base.
  • SI unit of mass? → Kilogram.
  • SI unit of weight? → Newton.
  • Weight formula? → W = mg.
  • Weight on Moon compared with Earth? → About one-sixth.
  • Does mass change on the Moon? → No.
  • Measure of inertia? → Mass.
  • SI unit of force? → Newton.
  • 1 newton? → 1 kg m/s².
  • Examples of non-contact forces? → Gravity, electrostatic and magnetic forces.
  • Surface force perpendicular to surface? → Normal reaction.
  • Does normal force always equal mg? → No.
  • Force transmitted through a rope? → Tension.
  • Force opposing relative motion? → Friction.
  • Maximum static friction? → Limiting friction.
  • Which is generally smaller: rolling or sliding friction? → Rolling friction.
  • Coefficient of friction unit? → No unit.
  • Internal resistance of fluid flow? → Viscosity.
  • SI unit of dynamic viscosity? → Pa s.
  • Terminal velocity means? → Constant maximum speed when forces balance in a fluid.
  • At terminal velocity acceleration? → Zero.
  • Pressure formula? → P = F/A.
  • SI unit of pressure? → Pascal.
  • 1 pascal? → 1 N/m².
  • For same force, smaller area produces? → Greater pressure.
  • Liquid-pressure formula? → P = ρgh.
  • Hydraulic machines work on? → Pascal's principle.
  • Upward force exerted by fluid? → Buoyant force.
  • Archimedes' Principle? → Buoyant force equals weight of displaced fluid.
  • Density formula? → ρ = m/V.
  • SI unit of density? → kg/m³.
  • Relative density has unit? → No.
  • Instrument measuring relative density of liquids? → Hydrometer.
  • Instrument associated with milk density? → Lactometer.
  • Turning effect of force? → Moment or torque.
  • Moment formula? → Force × perpendicular distance.
  • SI unit of torque? → N m.
  • Rotational equilibrium principle? → Clockwise moment = anticlockwise moment.
  • Fixed point of lever? → Fulcrum.
  • First-class lever has what in middle? → Fulcrum.
  • Second-class lever has what in middle? → Load.
  • Third-class lever has what in middle? → Effort.
  • Example of first-class lever? → Seesaw or scissors.
  • Example of second-class lever? → Wheelbarrow.
  • Example of third-class lever? → Human forearm with biceps.
  • Mechanical advantage formula? → Load/Effort.
  • Does mechanical advantage have a unit? → No.
  • Six simple machines? → Lever, wheel and axle, pulley, inclined plane, wedge and screw.
  • Fixed pulley mainly provides? → Change of force direction.
  • Movable pulley provides? → Mechanical advantage.
  • Can a machine create energy? → No.
  • Work formula? → W = Fs cos θ.
  • SI unit of work? → Joule.
  • When is mechanical work zero? → When displacement is zero or force is perpendicular to displacement.
  • Power formula? → W/t.
  • SI unit of power? → Watt.
  • 1 watt? → 1 joule per second.
  • 1 horsepower approximately? → 746 W.
  • Kinetic-energy formula? → ½mv².
  • If velocity doubles, kinetic energy becomes? → Four times.
  • Gravitational-potential-energy formula? → mgh.
  • Momentum formula? → p = mv.
  • SI unit of momentum? → kg m/s.
  • Impulse equals? → Change in momentum.
  • Impulse formula for constant force? → FΔt.
  • Why does an airbag reduce injury? → It increases collision time and reduces average force.
  • Momentum conserved in isolated collisions? → Yes.
  • Kinetic energy conserved in elastic collision? → Yes.
  • Kinetic energy conserved in inelastic collision? → No.
  • Perfectly inelastic collision means? → Bodies stick together.
  • Does constant-speed circular motion have acceleration? → Yes.
  • Direction of centripetal acceleration? → Toward centre.
  • Centripetal acceleration formula? → v²/r.
  • Centripetal-force formula? → mv²/r.
  • Is centripetal force a separate fundamental force? → No.
  • Centrifugal force in rotating frame? → Pseudo or apparent force.
  • Why are roads banked? → To assist provision of centripetal force and reduce dependence on friction.
  • Angular velocity SI unit? → rad/s.
  • Relation between linear and angular velocity? → v = rω.
  • Rotational analogue of mass? → Moment of inertia.
  • Angular momentum formula for rigid body? → L = Iω.
  • Angular momentum is conserved when? → External torque is zero.
  • In SHM, velocity maximum at? → Mean/equilibrium position.
  • In SHM, acceleration maximum at? → Extreme positions.
  • Simple pendulum period? → T = 2π√(L/g).
  • Does pendulum period depend on bob mass? → No, ideally.
  • Frequency formula? → f = 1/T.
  • SI unit of frequency? → Hertz.
  • Resonance occurs when? → Driving frequency is close to natural frequency.
  • Elasticity means? → Ability to regain original shape.
  • Stress formula? → Force/Area.
  • Stress SI unit? → Pascal.
  • Strain unit? → No unit.
  • Ratio of longitudinal stress to longitudinal strain? → Young's modulus.
  • Projectile path in ideal conditions? → Parabola.
  • At highest point of projectile, vertical velocity? → Zero.
  • At highest point, acceleration? → g downward.
  • Ideal maximum projectile range angle? → 45°.
  • Free fall means? → Motion under gravity alone.
  • Value of g near Earth's surface? → About 9.8 m/s².
  • Do heavier bodies fall faster in vacuum? → No.
  • Where is g approximately zero inside Earth? → Earth's centre.
  • Earth escape velocity? → About 11.2 km/s.
  • Near-Earth orbital velocity? → About 7.9 km/s.
  • Scientist who laid foundation of classical mechanics? → Isaac Newton.
  • Newton's Principia published? → 1687.
  • Scientist famous for studies of falling bodies? → Galileo Galilei.
  • Scientist associated with buoyancy and levers? → Archimedes.
